hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when someone says “anything but that,” what do you find yourself thinking about?
options: ha. me too. today’s story knows it.
good for you. today, a rule that was easy to keep, at first.

steps.line: God gave Adam and his wife a home: a garden. “Live in it,” He said, “and eat freely from it, wherever you like.”
The Qur’an describes the garden’s promise: no hunger there, no thirst, no going without clothes, no burning sun.

steps.q: Everything was theirs, with one limit: a single tree. How do you think the Qur’an words that limit?

steps.line: Then one limit: “Don’t come near this tree, or you will be wrongdoers.” Not even “don’t eat.” Don’t come near.

steps.q: Why might the rule be “don’t come near” instead of just “don’t eat”?
o: The tree was poisonous to touch
So they’d never learn what it was
Distance makes a limit easier to keep
steps.why: The closer you stand to a line, the easier it is to cross. Many teachers read the verse that way.

steps.q: The Qur’an never names the tree. Who does give it a name, and what name?
steps.why: Shaytan whispers that it’s “the tree of eternity, and a kingdom that never fades” (Qur’an 20:120). The only name it gets is a sales pitch.

steps.line: Notice what the Qur’an doesn’t say. It doesn’t name the tree, or the fruit. It doesn’t even name his wife. Later tradition calls her Hawwa, Eve.

steps.q: No fruit is named in the Qur’an. So where did the famous apple come from?
o: A Latin pun: malum, apple and evil
A later verse of the Qur’an names it
steps.why: Many scholars trace the apple to Latin, where malum means both “apple” and “evil.” Some Muslim commentators guessed wheat or grapes; many said if God left it unnamed, it doesn’t matter.

steps.line: Today, a friend lends you their apartment. Use the car, the books, the good coffee. Just don’t open the hall cupboard. Guess what you think about.
steps.label: today

steps.line: A hundred yeses, and one no. It’s an old joke which one keeps you up the first night.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. the yes came first, and it was huge. eat freely, wherever you like. the no was a single tree.
in islam, many scholars teach that things are allowed unless God has forbidden them. the limits are few, and the garden is wide.

steps.q: The permission came first, and the limit was one tree. What does that order suggest about God’s rules, in this story?
o: The gift is huge, the limit small inside it
The rules are the real point of the garden
The one tree mattered more than the rest
steps.why: Everything, minus one. The gift is the story. The limit is a small fence inside it.

today.say: today, count your garden before the tree. name five things you’re freely given and glad of, before the one thing you can’t have. if you like, end with alhamdulillah.
options: lovely. the yeses are usually bigger.
that’s plenty. the garden is wide.

tomorrow.title: The whisper.
tomorrow.line: someone starts to talk in the garden. not with a shout. with a whisper.

Qur’an 20:118-119 (no hunger, no nakedness, no thirst, no heat of the sun)
The legal maxim that things are permitted in origin (al-asl fi al-ashya’ al-ibaha): e.g. al-Suyuti, al-Ashbah wa al-Naza’ir
The name Hawwa: in the hadith (e.g. Sahih al-Bukhari 3330) and later tradition, not in the Qur’an
check: “Don’t come near” read as “keep your distance” is a common reading (e.g. in tafsir), not the only one. Confirm.
The permissibility maxim applies to things and dealings, not acts of worship; the teach line says “things.” Confirm.
